title: What Is a Michelin Star? Meaning, Ratings and How It Works
description: What a Michelin star means, what one, two and three stars stand for, how inspectors judge, where the stars came from and what a starred meal costs.
summary: What the stars mean, how inspectors judge, where they came from and what a starred meal costs.
keywords: what is a michelin star restaurant
body:
A Michelin star is an award the MICHELIN Guide gives restaurants for outstanding cooking, judged only on the food on the plate. Anonymous inspectors award one, two or three stars, three being the highest, and reassess every starred restaurant each year to make sure it still deserves them.

That short answer hides a system with more than a century of history, a precise set of judging criteria and a price ladder that climbs steeply with each star. Below we explain what each level means, how inspectors decide, where the stars came from and what a starred meal costs today, using the prices of the {{priced}} starred restaurants we track around the world.

Michelin star meaning: one, two and three stars

Every star is a verdict on the cooking, and the levels are cumulative: a two-star kitchen does everything a one-star kitchen does, with more personality and polish. Here is how the MICHELIN Guide describes each level today, alongside what a dinner tasting menu typically costs at that level.

The price gap between the levels is real. A two-star dinner typically costs about half as much again as a one-star dinner, and three stars roughly doubles the one-star price. Lunch is the classic way in: where a starred restaurant offers a set lunch, it typically costs {{lunch1}} at one star, {{lunch2}} at two and {{lunch3}} at three, often for a shorter version of the same cooking. A wine pairing adds about {{wine1}} at one star, {{wine2}} at two and {{wine3}} at three.

For decades the Guide summed up the levels in a single line each, and you will still see them quoted: one star meant “a very good restaurant in its category,” two stars “excellent cooking, worth a detour” and three stars “exceptional cuisine, worth a special journey.” The newer wording keeps the same ladder but puts the emphasis on the cooking rather than the trip.

Is three stars the highest Michelin star rating?

Yes. Three stars is the top of the scale, and there is no such thing as a four- or five-star Michelin restaurant. When people search for a “five-star” restaurant they are usually thinking of hotel ratings; Michelin’s own award for hotels is separate and uses Keys rather than stars. Only {{n3}} restaurants in the world hold three Michelin stars, about one in every {{oneIn3}} starred restaurants. {{top3Country}} has the most, with {{top3N}}, followed by {{second3Country}} with {{second3N}}. Our list of every three-Michelin-star restaurant names them all, with their prices.

What is a Michelin star restaurant? What inspectors judge

The MICHELIN Guide says its inspectors use the same five criteria everywhere in the world, so that a star in Tokyo means the same as a star in Paris or New York:

  1. The quality of the ingredients. Great cooking starts with great produce, from an heirloom tomato at its peak to well-raised meat and line-caught fish.
  2. The harmony of flavors. Every element on the plate should earn its place and work with the rest.
  3. Mastery of culinary techniques. Cooking times, seasoning, sauces and textures handled with precision, whether the style is classical or modern.
  4. The chef’s personality, expressed through the cuisine. A starred meal should taste like it could only come from that kitchen.
  5. Consistency, across the whole menu and over time. One brilliant dinner is not enough; the standard has to hold on every visit and every dish.

Just as telling is what the inspectors leave out. The Guide says decor, comfort and formality have no bearing on a star, and neither does the style of service or the wine list. That is why stars turn up in unexpected places: Bangkok street-food cook Jay Fai holds one, cooking crab omelets over charcoal in goggles, while a British pub, the Hand and Flowers in Marlow, holds two.

Inspectors are full-time Michelin employees, most of them former restaurant and hotel professionals, and they dine anonymously. A restaurant is visited as many times as it takes, by different inspectors, at lunch and dinner, on weekdays and weekends, before the team decides together. Each guide reveals its new stars once a year, usually at a ceremony attended by the chefs, and the changes take effect straight away. There is no quota: Michelin can award as many stars in a year as it finds deserving, and it can take them away just as freely. We go deeper into the process in How do restaurants get a Michelin star?

Michelin star origin: where the stars came from

The stars began as a marketing idea from a tire company. Brothers André and Édouard Michelin founded Michelin in Clermont-Ferrand, in central France, in 1889, when the country had fewer than 3,000 cars. To get more people driving (and wearing out tires), they published a free guide for motorists in 1900, with maps, tips on changing a tire, and lists of places to eat and stay.

  • 1900: the first MICHELIN Guide, given away free to drivers in France.
  • 1920: the Guide goes on sale for seven francs, drops paid advertising and adds restaurant listings by category. Michelin starts sending anonymous inspectors to review them.
  • 1926: the first stars, marking fine-dining restaurants with a single star.
  • 1931: the scale of one, two and three stars is introduced.
  • 1936: Michelin publishes the criteria behind each star level.
  • 1997: the Bib Gourmand arrives, for good food at moderate prices.
  • 2020: the Green Star is unveiled in the French guide, for restaurants leading on sustainability.
  • 2026: Michelin announces the Green Star will be phased out, replaced by Mindful Voices, an editorial platform profiling chefs, hoteliers and wine producers.

The little red book has since grown into a global guide covering more than 50 destinations, with selections published online and in an app as well as in print. Dates are from the MICHELIN Guide’s own history of the Guide.

Michelin star vs Bib Gourmand vs Green Star

A Bib Gourmand is not a star. It marks restaurants serving high-quality cooking at a good price, usually simpler food without luxury ingredients. The price ceiling varies from country to country with the cost of living, but the idea is the same everywhere: a meal that feels like a bargain for the quality. More than 3,000 restaurants hold one, and a Bib restaurant can later earn a star. We compare the two in Bib Gourmand vs Michelin star.

The Green Star sat alongside the red stars rather than above or below them. It recognized restaurants at the forefront of sustainable gastronomy: working closely with local farmers and fishers, cooking with the seasons, cutting waste and single-use plastic. A restaurant could hold red stars and a Green Star at the same time, or a Green Star alone. In May 2026 Michelin announced that the Green Star is being phased out, so fewer restaurants will show one as each guide publishes its next edition. See the Green Michelin Star explained.

Which countries have Michelin stars?

There are {{total}} Michelin-starred restaurants in {{countries}} countries and territories, on every continent except Africa and Antarctica. {{topCountry}} leads with {{topCountryN}}, followed by {{secondCountry}} ({{secondCountryN}}) and {{thirdCountry}} ({{thirdCountryN}}). Some well-fed countries have none simply because Michelin doesn’t publish a guide there yet: Australia and India are the best-known examples. Our world map shows every starred restaurant, and Michelin stars by country has the full count.

To see what a star costs in a particular city, start with one of our most-visited destinations: Paris, Tokyo, New York and London each list every starred restaurant with its dinner, lunch and wine pairing prices side by side.

The Michelin star symbol and logo

The Michelin star logo is not a five-pointed star. The symbol is a rounded, flower-like shape with six petals around a hollow center, which French diners nickname a macaron. It appears in red next to each starred restaurant in the Guide, on its website and in its app, repeated once, twice or three times. The Bib Gourmand has its own symbol, the face of Bibendum, the Michelin Man, licking his lips, and the Green Star, now being phased out, is a green version of the star.

Restaurants often show the symbol on a plaque by the door or on their own websites, but the only reliable place to check a restaurant’s current rating is the MICHELIN Guide itself, since stars change every year.

faq.q: Can a restaurant lose a Michelin star?
faq.a: Yes. Stars are not permanent: inspectors reassess every starred restaurant each year, and if the cooking is no longer at the same level, the star is not renewed in the next edition. Restaurants also lose stars when they close, move or change hands, and a few chefs have asked to be removed from the Guide. Each destination on The Starred Bill marks recent gains and losses under Show › Recent star changes.

faq.q: Does the chef or the restaurant hold the Michelin star?
faq.a: The restaurant. Michelin awards stars to restaurants, not to chefs, so a chef who moves on does not take the star with them. When the head chef changes, inspectors return as often as needed to decide whether to keep, raise or lower the rating.

faq.q: How much does a Michelin-star meal cost?
faq.a: Across the restaurants we track, a dinner tasting menu typically costs about {{price1}} per person at one star, {{price2}} at two stars and {{price3}} at three stars, before service and drinks. The cheapest starred menus cost well under $100, and lunch menus are often cheaper still. Prices vary widely by city, so check each destination page for local prices.

faq.q: How many Michelin stars can a restaurant have?
faq.a: Three at most. One, two and three stars are the only levels, and three stars is the highest rating Michelin gives. {{n3}} restaurants in the world hold three stars.

faq.q: Is a Michelin-recommended restaurant the same as a Michelin-starred one?
faq.a: No. Being listed in the MICHELIN Guide means inspectors recommend a restaurant for good cooking, and only a small share of those listed restaurants go on to hold stars. Stars, Bib Gourmands and plain listings are three different levels of recognition, so check for the star symbol next to a restaurant’s name.

faq.q: Do restaurants pay or apply for a Michelin star?
faq.a: No restaurant can buy a star. Restaurants already in the Guide are reassessed continuously, and while any restaurant can ask to be considered, inspectors decide for themselves where to eat and pay no attention to who asked.
